Katherine Heigl stars as Abby, a supposedly intelligent television news producer working in Sacramento, whose show is struggling to stay afloat in the ratings. Presented as a competent and ambitious professional, Abby finds herself under mounting pressure to reverse her program's declining fortunes.

In an attempt to boost viewership, her boss brings in Mike, played by Gerard Butler, a crude cable personality whose show trades in reductive, sexist advice about relationships between men and women. His brash, provocative style stands in stark contrast to Abby's more measured sensibilities, setting the stage for the film's central conflict.

Although Abby is initially skeptical of Mike's outrageous approach, his surprising popularity with Sacramento audiences quickly proves her wrong. During the crucial ratings sweeps, his segments draw in viewers and revive the show's flagging numbers, forcing Abby to confront the uncomfortable success of his methods.

What makes the film particularly disappointing is that, despite being written by three female screenwriters, it ultimately endorses Mike's dated and sexist worldview rather than challenging it. This uncritical embrace of outdated gender politics undermines the comedy, leaving the film unable to generate genuine laughs.

Directed by Robert Luketic, the movie makes little effort to conceal its derivative and formulaic nature. From its predictable romantic-comedy beats to its familiar odd-couple dynamic, the film offers little in the way of originality, coasting instead on well-worn conventions that fail to elevate the material.

# The Ugly Truth: A Comedy That Betrays Its Own Premise

"The Ugly Truth," a modern screwball comedy directed by Robert Luketic, centers on Abby Richter (Katherine Heigl), a neurotic and controlling television producer whose meticulously ordered life leaves little room for romance. When her struggling morning show hires Mike Chadway (Gerard Butler), a crude cable personality who dispenses blunt and cynical relationship advice, Abby finds herself professionally bound to a man whose worldview she finds repugnant. The film's central engine is set in motion when Mike, sensing an opportunity, offers to coach the perpetually single Abby in the art of seduction—specifically to help her win over Colin (Eric Winter), the handsome doctor who has recently moved in next door. In exchange, Abby agrees to keep Mike on the show if his methods succeed in landing her the man of her dreams.

On paper, this setup contains all the ingredients of a classic battle-of-the-sexes comedy, a genre that thrives on witty adversaries whose sparring eventually reveals mutual attraction. The great screwball comedies of Hollywood's golden age succeeded because they pitted equally matched partners against one another, allowing sharp dialogue and comic reversals to expose the pretensions of both parties. One might reasonably expect "The Ugly Truth" to follow this tradition, using Abby's intelligence to puncture and ultimately dismantle Mike's reductive theories about men and women.

Yet the film squanders this potential in a remarkable act of self-sabotage. Despite being written by three female screenwriters—a fact that makes its failures all the more disappointing—the movie ultimately endorses rather than subverts Mike's tired sexist philosophy. Instead of proving him wrong, the narrative bends over backward to prove him right. Abby's transformation is not one of growth or self-discovery but of capitulation: she learns to suppress her ambition, dumb down her conversation, and reshape herself entirely to fit the crude template of male desire that Mike prescribes. The film's most infamous set piece, in which Abby unknowingly wears vibrating underwear to a business dinner, reduces her from a competent professional to an object of humiliation played for cheap laughs.

The tragedy of "The Ugly Truth" is that it mistakes cynicism for honesty and crudeness for truth-telling. Rather than challenging its protagonist to remain true to herself while finding love, it insists that a woman must abandon her authentic identity to be worthy of romance. What could have been a sharp critique of retrograde gender politics instead becomes an unwitting celebration of them, leaving audiences with neither the wit of genuine comedy nor the satisfaction of an earned romance.

When she finally landed her first internship at a regional news station, she felt she was on her way. But her early days in the industry brought unexpected challenges. During her first live report, Katherine froze on camera. The words she had rehearsed dozens of times vanished from her mind. The silence stretched for what felt like an eternity before her producer cut to a commercial break.

The **humiliation** was overwhelming. Katherine was certain her career had ended before it even began. Colleagues offered sympathetic smiles, but she could barely meet their eyes. She spent the drive home replaying the moment, wondering if she had made a terrible mistake pursuing this path.

That evening, however, she received an unexpected email from a senior editor. He wrote about his own disastrous first broadcast years earlier—how he too had frozen, forgotten his lines, and wanted to quit. "Everyone stumbles," he explained. Encouraged, Katherine returned to work the next day determined to grow. She practiced relentlessly, studied the techniques of veteran reporters, and gradually rebuilt her confidence. Weeks later, when she delivered a flawless report on a local story, her producer gave her an approving nod.

The experience taught Katherine that failure and embarrassment are not endpoints—they are part of the journey. Years later, whenever she mentored young journalists, she shared her own story of that painful first broadcast, reminding them that even the reporters they admired on **CNN** had once faced their own moments of doubt and struggle.

# 'The Ugly Truth' Peddles Ugly Stereotypes in Rom-Com Clothing

**CNN Review**

There's a moment in "The Ugly Truth" when you realize the film isn't just failing to transcend the tired conventions of the romantic comedy—it's actively dragging the genre backward, kicking and screaming, into territory that feels genuinely regressive.

Katherine Heigl stars as Abby Richter, a controlling, career-obsessed television producer whose life is upended when her station hires Mike Chadway (Gerard Butler), a crude cable personality who has built a following by telling women the "ugly truth": that men are simple creatures interested only in physical attraction, and that women must play manipulative games to snare them.

## A Chemistry Problem

Let's start with what should be the beating heart of any romantic comedy—the central pairing. Heigl and Butler share little of the electric tension that made classics like "When Harry Met Sally" sing. Butler, so commanding in "300," seems stranded here, delivering misogynistic monologues with a smirk that the film mistakes for charm. Heigl, meanwhile, is asked to play the uptight harridan who simply needs a "real man" to loosen her up.

The problem isn't the actors' talent. It's that the screenplay gives them nothing genuine to build upon.

## The Real Ugly Truth

The film's central thesis is its most troubling feature. Chadway's worldview—that women should suppress their intelligence, dress provocatively, and manipulate men into commitment—is presented initially as controversial, but the narrative ultimately validates it. When Abby follows his advice and lands her dream man, the movie suggests that authenticity and self-respect are obstacles to romance.

There's an infamous sequence involving vibrating underwear at a business dinner that epitomizes the film's approach: crude for shock value, humiliating for its female lead, and desperate for laughs it hasn't earned.

## Gender Politics Stuck in Reverse

What's most disappointing is how the film squanders its potential. A smarter movie might have used Chadway's provocations to actually interrogate gender dynamics. Instead, "The Ugly Truth" endorses the very cynicism it pretends to critique. Abby's professional competence is treated as a character flaw. Her transformation into a more "desirable" woman requires her to become less herself.

The R-rating suggests edginess, but there's nothing bold about recycling the notion that career women are secretly miserable and merely need the right man to fix them.

## The Verdict

"The Ugly Truth" wants to have it both ways—celebrating raunchy honesty while delivering a conventional happy ending. The result satisfies neither impulse. Heigl deserves better material, and audiences deserve romantic comedies that respect their intelligence.

The ugliest truth of all? This is a missed opportunity dressed up as a comedy.

**Rating: 1.5 out of 4 stars**

# The Ugly Truth About "The Ugly Truth"

There's a particular species of romantic comedy that mistakes crudeness for wit and calls it progressive—as if a woman being allowed to hear the word "orgasm" repeatedly constitutes a great leap forward for the genre. "The Ugly Truth" is the apex predator of this species, a film so pleased with its own supposed edginess that it never notices it's telling the same tired story with fresher profanity.

## A Screwball Comedy Missing the Actual Screws

Let's be generous and grant the film its aspirations. It clearly wants to be a modern "His Girl Friday," pairing a sparring man and woman whose antagonism masks attraction. But the great screwball comedies understood something this movie fundamentally doesn't: the battle of the sexes only works when both combatants are actually *armed*.

Katherine Hepburn traded barbs with Cary Grant as an equal—smarter, faster, and frequently victorious. The genre's engine ran on genuine parity. "The Ugly Truth" instead rigs the fight from the opening bell. Every witty observation belongs to Mike, the crass TV personality. Every pratfall, every humiliation, every moment of being *wrong* belongs to Abby.

That's not screwball. That's just one character screwing another over for ninety minutes.

## Katherine Heigl Deserved a Better Truth

Here's where the film curdles from merely lazy into something genuinely uncomfortable. Abby, our female lead, is introduced as a competent, successful television producer. Within reels, the movie systematically dismantles her—not through organic character growth, but through a relentless campaign insisting that her problem is that she's *too* controlling, *too* particular, *too* much herself.

The film's actual thesis is grotesque when stated plainly: a woman's standards are her character flaw. Abby doesn't need to grow; she needs to *shrink*—to abandon her checklist, wear the vibrating panties, and let a boorish man reshape her into someone more palatable. Her arc isn't self-discovery; it's self-diminishment.

Meanwhile, Mike learns... what, exactly? That he has feelings after all? He's rewarded for his cynicism with the very woman he spent the movie mocking. His crudeness is charming; her competence is a liability. He gets to be right about everything and *also* get the girl. Some negotiation.

## The Chemistry Experiment That Never Ignites

None of this would sting quite so badly if the leads generated actual heat. Gerard Butler smirks through the role like a man who's read the script and knows he's the protected party. Heigl, a genuinely gifted comic actress, is forced to spend the runtime being flustered, embarrassed, and progressively defeated—hardly the stuff romantic sparks are made of.

The infamous restaurant scene, in which Mike feeds Abby lines during a date, might be the film in miniature: a woman literally reduced to a puppet, mouthing a man's words to win another man's approval. We're meant to find it delightful. It plays like a horror movie.

## The Verdict

"The Ugly Truth" wants credit for honesty it never earns. The genuinely ugly truth is that beneath its raunchy veneer beats the heart of the most retrograde message imaginable: that women should stop being so *demanding* and settle for the man who insults them.

The screwball masters would have handed Abby the sharper knife. This film hands her a script written by the man who's mocking her—and calls that a love story.

**One star**, awarded entirely for Heigl's doomed effort to make chicken salad from material that was something else entirely.

# The Ugly Truth: A Crude Retread of Battle-of-the-Sexes Comedies

**Rated R | 96 minutes | Directed by Robert Luketic**

There was a time when the war between men and women played out with wit sharp enough to draw blood without ever spilling a drop of vulgarity. In the golden age of screwball comedy, verbal sparring was an art form, and the sexual tension between adversaries crackled with intelligence. "The Ugly Truth," directed by Robert Luketic, aspires to that lineage but settles for something considerably coarser, trading rapier repartee for raunch and mistaking crudeness for candor.

The premise, at least, carries echoes of a nobler tradition. Abby Richter (Katherine Heigl) is a high-strung Sacramento morning-show producer whose meticulously controlled life is upended by Mike Chadway (Gerard Butler), a boorish television personality whose "Ugly Truth" segment reduces romance to a series of cynical, testosterone-fueled pronouncements. When Mike is hired to boost Abby's flagging ratings, the two clash immediately—she the buttoned-up idealist, he the swaggering realist. Naturally, opposites are destined to attract.

One can almost see the ghost of a better film here. The setup recalls the delicious antagonism of Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy in "Woman of the Year" (1942), where a mismatched pair of professionals sparred across the gender divide with equal measures of pride and vulnerability. Hepburn, in particular, built a career on playing formidable women who met their intellectual match rather than their master. Think of her verbal fencing with Cary Grant in "Bringing Up Baby" or her regal unraveling in "The Philadelphia Story." Those films understood that the most electric comedy arises from equals in genuine combat.

"The Ugly Truth," by contrast, stacks the deck. Heigl, a gifted comic actress capable of real warmth, is saddled with a character who exists primarily to be humiliated and corrected. Abby's neuroses are the film's punchline, and her eventual capitulation to Mike's worldview feels less like romance than surrender. Where Hepburn's heroines gave as good as they got, Abby is repeatedly positioned as the one who must learn, loosen up, and, in the film's most infamous sequence, don a pair of vibrating underwear to a business dinner. It is a scene engineered for shock rather than laughter, and it exemplifies the movie's fatal miscalculation.

That R rating is earned not through mature emotional honesty but through a relentless barrage of anatomical frankness. The screenplay, credited to three writers, seems convinced that the surest route to laughs runs through the gutter. There are moments—a few sharp exchanges, a well-timed reaction shot—when the film's better instincts surface. Butler, working against his usual action-hero grain, brings a rough charm to Mike, and his chemistry with Heigl occasionally sparks. But the material rarely rises to meet them.

Compare this to "It Happened One Night" (1934), Frank Capra's template for nearly every romantic comedy that followed, in which Clark Gable and Claudette Colbert bickered their way to love with impeccable timing and not a single crude flourish. That film trusted its audience to find the humor in restraint, in the electricity of the unspoken. "The Ugly Truth" trusts nothing, spelling out every innuendo and underlining every joke until it goes limp.

At a brisk 96 minutes, the film at least does not overstay its welcome, and Luketic—who demonstrated a lighter touch with "Legally Blonde"—keeps things moving efficiently. The Sacramento newsroom setting offers a mildly amusing backdrop of ratings desperation and on-air antics, and the supporting cast performs gamely. But efficiency is not the same as inspiration, and the film's climactic gestures toward genuine feeling arrive too late to redeem what precedes them.

The tragedy of "The Ugly Truth" is that it possesses the raw ingredients for something better: two appealing leads, a proven director, and a premise as old and reliable as the movies themselves. What it lacks is faith—faith that audiences might prefer wit to shock, partnership to conquest, and heroines who remain the equals of the men they eventually embrace.

Katharine Hepburn once observed that the best relationships are between people who challenge each other. The classic comedies she helped define understood this instinctively. "The Ugly Truth" gestures toward that ideal, then buries it beneath a mountain of cheap gags.

**Rating: ★★ out of ★★★★**

# Love, Actually Regressive: A Review of *The Ugly Truth* (2009)

There's a moment in *The Ugly Truth* where you realize the film's title is doing more heavy lifting than Gerard Butler's ab workout: the ugly truth is that Hollywood spent a decade watching *When Harry Met Sally* and learned exactly none of its lessons.

## The Setup

Katherine Heigl plays Abby Richter, a control-freak TV producer whose personality is "has a checklist for men" and whose character arc is "learns to abandon standards." Enter Mike Chadway (Butler), a cable troglodyte whose entire philosophy is that women are manipulable meat-puppets and men are simple beasts governed by their groins. He is, naturally, positioned as the one who *understands love*.

## The Sexist Double Standard, Itemized

Here's the arithmetic that doesn't add up. Abby is punished by the narrative for having preferences—she's "uptight," "impossible," "going to die alone." Mike is *rewarded* for being crude, because his cynicism is packaged as refreshing honesty. She wants a partner who meets criteria; he wants a woman who shuts up and wears the right jeans. Guess which one the film treats as neurotic?

The message lands with all the subtlety of a brick: a woman with standards needs fixing, while a man with contempt just needs the love of a good woman to soften him. Abby must transform. Mike must merely *show up*.

## The Scene We Need to Talk About

Then comes the vibrating-underwear-in-a-restaurant sequence—a woman losing physical control of herself at a business dinner while a child works the remote. It's staged as the film's comic centerpiece, and it's clearly reaching for the famous deli scene in *When Harry Met Sally*.

But notice the crucial inversion. In Rob Reiner's film, Sally *chooses* to perform her fake orgasm. It's a woman weaponizing wit to make a point about male cluelessness—**she** holds all the power, and the punchline ("I'll have what she's having") belongs to her. In *The Ugly Truth*, Abby's ecstasy is involuntary, engineered by external forces, witnessed and controlled by others. Agency versus accident. Nora Ephron gave her heroine the microphone; this film puts a remote in someone else's hand.

That's the whole problem in miniature.

## The Verdict

Butler and Heigl have enough chemistry to suggest a better movie was theoretically possible, which almost makes it worse. Instead we get a film that mistakes cynicism for insight and humiliation for romance.

*When Harry Met Sally* asked whether men and women could be friends. *The Ugly Truth* isn't even sure they should be allowed in the same restaurant.

**★★☆☆☆** — Two stars, both for the actors' doomed attempt to elevate the material.

# The Ugly Truth: A Romantic Comedy That Forgets to Respect Its Heroine

There's a particular kind of disappointment that comes from watching two talented actors trapped in a screenplay that doesn't deserve them. "The Ugly Truth" is exactly that kind of movie—a supposedly romantic comedy that mistakes cruelty for chemistry and humiliation for humor.

## The Setup

Katherine Heigl plays Abby Richter, a control-freak morning news producer in Sacramento whose personal life is as meticulously organized as her segment rundowns. She has checklists for her ideal man and a habit of googling her dates before meeting them. Enter Mike Chadway (Gerard Butler), a crude cable personality whose show "The Ugly Truth" preaches a cynical, reductive philosophy: men are simple creatures interested only in physical appearance, and women should stop pretending otherwise.

When Mike is hired onto Abby's struggling station to boost ratings, the two clash immediately. But the plot machinery soon forces them together: Abby develops a crush on her handsome doctor neighbor, and Mike offers to coach her in the art of seduction according to his crass rulebook. Cue the makeovers, the push-up bras, and the dating advice designed to reduce Abby to a performance of male fantasy.

## Where It Goes Wrong

The film's central problem isn't its premise—plenty of good romantic comedies feature bickering opposites. The problem is how thoroughly the movie enjoys degrading its heroine while giving its male lead a free pass.

Consider the film's most infamous sequence, in which Abby unknowingly wears vibrating underwear controlled by a remote that ends up in a child's hands, causing her to writhe and moan through a business dinner. It's a scene engineered purely to humiliate her, played for laughs at her expense. Throughout the film, Abby is the butt of the joke: she's mocked for being uptight, punished for having standards, and repeatedly told that her intelligence and independence are precisely what's keeping her alone.

Mike, meanwhile, faces no such reckoning. His misogynistic worldview is treated as roguish charm rather than a genuine character flaw requiring growth. The screenplay barely asks him to change; instead, it validates his cynical philosophy by having his advice *work*. The message lands with a thud: Abby was wrong to be herself, and Mike was right all along.

## The Uncomfortable Truth About "The Ugly Truth"

A better film might have used this dynamic to actually challenge Mike's worldview—to prove him wrong and reward Abby's authenticity. Instead, the movie asks us to believe these two belong together while never establishing why Abby would want a man who spent the entire film insulting women like her.

Heigl commits fully and has genuine comic timing; Butler is charismatic enough that you wish he'd been handed a character worth rooting for. But their efforts can't overcome a script that seems fundamentally contemptuous of its female lead. The chemistry the film insists upon never materializes because the relationship is built on his condescension and her self-abasement.

## The Verdict

"The Ugly Truth" wants to be a naughty, R-rated update of the battle-of-the-sexes comedy. What it delivers instead is a mean-spirited exercise in putting a smart woman in her place. The real ugly truth is that this movie doesn't like women very much—and it certainly doesn't like Abby, the person we're supposed to be cheering for.

**★☆☆☆☆ (1 out of 5 stars)**

*Skip it, and revisit "When Harry Met Sally" instead—a film that understood you can have sparks without the cruelty.*
